sections.authorBiography: Ambrose Bierce was born in Meigs County, Ohio, on 24 June 1842. He fought for the Union in the Civil War, at Shiloh and Chickamauga, and was seriously wounded in the head at Kennesaw Mountain in 1864. Afterwards he became a sharp-tongued San Francisco journalist and columnist, known as "Bitter Bierce," and wrote war stories and ghost stories collected in Tales of Soldiers and Civilians (1891) and the satirical Devil's Dictionary (1906; 1911). In late 1913 he travelled into revolutionary Mexico and disappeared; his fate is unknown.
sections.historicalContext: The story is set in northern Alabama during the American Civil War (1861–1865). Union forces held railroads in the region and executed civilians caught sabotaging them. Bierce had fought for the Union at Shiloh and Chickamauga, and his war stories are known for their unsentimental view of death.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Peyton Farquhar was dead; his body, with a broken neck, swung gently from side to side beneath the timbers of the Owl Creek bridge” slowly and put it in my own words: The last sentence tells us flatly that Farquhar was dead, his body swinging under the bridge. Next, craft. I notice the calm, factual words ("was dead," "swung gently") come right after pages of rushing escape, so the flat tone itself is the shock. The strongest word is “gently”: it is a soft, almost peaceful word set beside "a broken neck," and the clash makes the ending colder. Then, effect. What does this sentence reveal about how Bierce built the whole story? My answer: Bierce, a Civil War veteran, writes the escape as a dream and then states the hard fact plainly; the whole story is a trap about how war treats a hopeful mind.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the story to illusion and reality.

middleSchool.label: Scaffolded support
middleSchool.text: Supported track: write a five-paragraph essay explaining what An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge teaches about illusion and reality. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Ambrose Bierce develops illusion and reality in An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Ambrose Bierce develops illusion and reality across An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of illusion and reality. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of illusion and reality in An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Ambrose Bierce's choices in An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of illusion and reality, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge's treatment of illusion and reality in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on illusion and reality in An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
